seoTitle: How to Set Up a Domain in Google Workspace (2026)
metaDescription: Learn how to add and set up a new domain in Google Workspace in 2026, from entering domain details to verifying ownership correctly.
intro: Adding a domain to Google Workspace is the foundation for getting a professional email address and using Google's tools under your own brand. This guide covers how to add a new domain and get it fully set up.

steps.heading: Navigate to domain settings
steps.body: In the Admin Console, find the Domains section where you can view existing domains and add a new one.

steps.heading: Add your new domain
steps.body: Enter the domain name exactly as registered with your domain provider, choosing whether it's a primary domain or a secondary one.

steps.heading: Verify domain ownership
steps.body: Google requires proof that you own the domain, typically through a DNS TXT record or HTML file upload provided by your registrar.

steps.heading: Configure the correct settings
steps.body: Once verified, review the domain's settings to make sure it's connected correctly and ready to support email and other Workspace services.

steps.heading: Apply any useful setup tips
steps.body: Double-check DNS propagation and settings before relying on the domain for live email, since changes can take time to fully take effect.

faq.question: How long does domain verification take in Google Workspace?
faq.answer: Verification is often quick once the DNS record is added, but propagation can take anywhere from a few minutes to 48 hours depending on your provider.

faq.question: Can I add more than one domain to Google Workspace?
faq.answer: Yes, Workspace supports adding multiple domains and domain aliases under the same account.

faq.question: Do I need to change my domain registrar to use Google Workspace?
faq.answer: No, you can keep your existing registrar and just update the DNS records to point to Google Workspace's services.

faq.question: What happens if domain verification fails?
faq.answer: Double-check that the TXT record or HTML file matches exactly what Google provided, and allow time for DNS changes to propagate before retrying.
